platforms.title: Dizziness That Hits Only When You Move Your Head
platforms.meta_description: BPPV causes brief spinning only when you move your head a certain way. How to tell it apart from other dizziness and when it becomes an emergency.
platforms.body_html:
Ever rolled over in bed or looked up to grab something off a shelf and suddenly felt the room spin? The Vestibular Disorders Association flags that pattern as classic for BPPV — benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Unlike dizziness that lingers no matter what you're doing, this kind hits hard and briefly, and only with certain head movements.

Why moving your head sets it off

The inner ear's vestibular system contains tiny calcium carbonate crystals called otoconia that normally help sense head position, but when they dislodge and drift into the semicircular canals, they cause trouble. Every time you move your head a certain way, those loose crystals shift inside the canal and send the brain a false signal of spinning. The world feels like it's whirling even though you're not actually moving, and the sensation usually passes within seconds to about a minute.

According to the Vestibular Disorders Association, the biggest risk factors are a head injury, age-related degeneration, prolonged bed rest, and other inner ear conditions. Lying down for extended periods actually makes it easier for crystals to dislodge in the first place, which means staying in bed to avoid triggering dizziness can ironically slow recovery down.

How to tell it apart from other dizziness, and how it's treated

First, dizziness that lasts seconds to about a minute, repeats with specific head movements, and comes without ringing in the ears or hearing loss. That's a clearly different pattern from Ménière's disease, which brings hearing changes and can last for hours at a time.

Second, dizziness that shows up alongside a severe headache, double vision, slurred speech, or sudden weakness in the arms or legs. That combination isn't BPPV — it can signal a stroke, and it calls for emergency care right away rather than waiting to see if it passes.

Without either of those red flags, BPPV responds remarkably well to a canalith repositioning procedure, commonly called the Epley maneuver. A doctor or physical therapist guides the head through a specific sequence of movements that coaxes the displaced crystals back where they belong, and many people see major improvement after just one or two sessions.

It can come back, though, and that's normal rather than a sign the first treatment failed. Crystals can dislodge again months or years later, especially after another head bump or simply with age, so a repeat episode usually just means booking another repositioning session rather than starting over from scratch. Some clinics also teach a version of the maneuver to do at home for future flare-ups, once the diagnosis has been confirmed by a specialist ahead of time.

The takeaway: brief spinning triggered by a specific head movement is worth suspecting as BPPV. A severe headache or slurred speech alongside it means the ER, not a wait-and-see approach — otherwise, an ear, nose, and throat specialist can confirm it and start repositioning treatment. This article is for general health information; consult a medical professional for diagnosis and treatment.
